en: Observers in Legazpi City can clearly see the nearly perfect symmetrical cone shape of Mayon Volcano in Albay, formed by repeated ash and lava eruptions.
Stalactites and stalagmites visibly form inside the Puerto Princesa Underground River cave as dripping mineral-rich water deposits calcite over thousands of years.
Taal Lake in Batangas visibly changes color from blue to green or red depending on the specific types of algae blooming in its waters.
The giant Rafflesia flower in Philippine rainforests is easily observable by its massive red petals and its strong, distinct smell of rotting meat.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol turn brown during the dry season because the dry heat turns the green grass covering the limestone mounds brown.
During the amihan season, the northeast monsoon winds visibly push dry, cool air across the country, causing clear skies and lower humidity in the atmosphere.
Snorkelers off the coast of Moalboal can visibly watch millions of silver sardines swimming in massive, swirling schools to protect themselves from predators.
The reddish-brown laterite soil visible in Surigao del Norte contains high concentrations of nickel, a valuable metal extracted from the earth for industrial use.
The Banaue Rice Terraces visibly follow the natural contour lines of the Cordillera mountains, creating flat, stair-like ponds that hold water for growing rice.
The Philippine tarsier in Bohol forests has enormous eyes that are larger than its brain, allowing it to visibly spot insects in the dark.
The dense mangrove forests visible along the coast of Panguil Bay have exposed aerial roots that poke out of the mud to help the trees breathe.
Visitors to the Tiwi Geothermal Field in Albay can observe hot steam visibly rising from the ground and boiling mud pots bubbling naturally.
